PT-P2 Neural Network Training¶

This notebook follows the lecture section order and adapts the code to the PT-P2 dataset stored in Google Drive.

Introduction: What this notebook is, how it's organized, and why¶

What. This notebook is the PT-P2 deliverable: it takes the same customer-sentiment dataset used in the no-code PT-P1 exercise and re-builds a classifier for it in Keras, so the two approaches (no-code heuristics vs. hand-tuned Python/TensorFlow) can be compared directly. It trains one 3-class text classifier (Positive_Praise / Negative_Complaint / Urgent_Support) across 16 separate runs and logs each run's hyperparameters and metrics.

How it's organized. The notebook follows the assignment's Task 1-4 structure, and every experiment reuses the same 4-part cell pattern:

  1. Hyperparameter Configuration + Architecture — a CONFIG dict (grouped into the lecture's 3 Pillars: Architecture, Optimization, Regularization) followed by the Keras Sequential model built from it.
  2. Optimizer & Compilation + Fit/Evaluate — builds the optimizer, compiles the model, trains it with .fit(), then computes weighted F1/precision/recall on the validation set.
  3. Loss Curve Chart — plots and saves train-vs-validation loss so the run can be diagnosed as underfitting, overfitting, or a good fit.

Task 1 (EXP-01) replicates the assignment's default baseline settings. Task 2 (EXP-02-EXP-05) deliberately induces underfitting, then overfitting, then tests regularization, then a custom config — each one isolating a specific lecture concept. Task 4 (EXP-05A-EXP-05J) is a one-variable-at- a-time ablation chain: each run changes exactly one lever off a shared baseline (EXP-05C, which combines the two things that helped independently — early stopping and expanded data) so that any change in the result can be attributed to one specific cause rather than a bundle of simultaneous changes.

Why this structure. The exercise's real goal isn't just to run Keras — it's to outperform the PT-P1 no-code benchmark (90.0% accuracy on clear phrasing, 33.3%→43.3% on sarcastic/ambiguous phrasing after refinement) while being able to explain why each configuration change helped or hurt, in terms of the three hyperparameter pillars and the bias/variance tradeoff the lecture covers. One-variable-at-a-time ablation is what makes those explanations defensible rather than guesswork: if two hyperparameters change at once and the result improves, there's no way to know which change actually mattered.

What this cell does: Mounts Google Drive (where the CSVs and saved loss-curve PNGs live) and imports every library used later in the notebook.

How:

  • drive.mount('/content/drive') gives this Colab session read/write access to the PT-P2 Neural Network Training folder in Drive, so later cells can load pt_p1_dataset.csv and save loss-curve images there.
  • pandas/numpy handle the CSV data and array math.
  • Sequential, Embedding, GlobalAveragePooling1D, Dense, Dropout from tensorflow.keras are the exact building blocks used to construct every model in this notebook.
  • Adam, SGD are the two optimizers Task 2/4 compare (Pillar 2: Optimization).
  • train_test_split performs the 70/15/15 train/val/test partition the exercise requires.
  • f1_score, accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score compute the metrics the training log needs (average='weighted' is used later so metrics account for class support).
  • Counter is used inside the custom tokenizer to count word frequencies when building the vocabulary.
  • matplotlib.pyplot draws the loss curves.
  • np.random.seed(42) / tf.random.set_seed(42) fix the random number generators up front.

Why: Every experiment cell later in the notebook re-applies these same two seed calls right before building its model. Doing it here and per-experiment means each run's weight initialization is controlled as tightly as TensorFlow allows, which matters because the "Random Seed" column in the experiment log is only meaningful if runs are actually reproducible enough to compare against each other.

Mounted at /content/drive

Load & Preprocess CSV Data¶

What this cell does: Loads the PT-P1 dataset, turns the raw text into fixed-length integer sequences a neural network can actually take as input, and splits everything into train/validation/test sets.

How, line by line:

  • CSV_FILEPATH points at the same 332-row dataset used in PT-P1, so PT-P2's results are directly comparable to that benchmark.
  • MAX_LEN = 20 caps every input at 20 tokens (longer sentences get truncated, shorter ones padded) — Keras needs every input to be the same shape.
  • MAX_VOCAB_SIZE = 1000 caps how many distinct words get their own vocabulary slot.
  • build_vocab() lower-cases and splits every sentence into words, counts frequency with Counter, and keeps only the most common MAX_VOCAB_SIZE - 2 words — the -2 reserves index 0 for a <PAD> token and index 1 for <UNK> (any word that didn't make the cut), so every possible word maps to some integer even if it's rare or unseen.
  • text_to_sequence() converts one sentence into a list of vocabulary indices, then pads with zeros or truncates to exactly MAX_LEN tokens.
  • vocab = build_vocab(...) / encoded_texts = [...] apply those two functions across the whole dataset, producing X_data (the numeric feature matrix) and y_data (the integer labels).
  • train_test_split is called twice: first splits 70% train / 30% "temp", then splits that temp set 50/50 into validation and test — together giving the required 70%/15%/15% partition.

Why: This is the "feature extraction" step the lecture and PT-P1 report both point to — a neural network can't do math on raw words, so this cell is the translation layer that turns labeled text into numbers before any training can happen. The exact 70/15/15 split matches Slide 6 ("Dataset Partitioning and Preprocessing") and the assignment's Task 1 requirement, and keeping a strictly isolated test set (never touched during training or hyperparameter tuning) is what makes the final evaluation trustworthy rather than optimistic.

Dataset shape: (332, 3)
Columns: ['text', 'label', 'category']
Classes: 3
Train/Val/Test shapes: (232, 20) (50, 20) (50, 20)

Hyperparameter Configuration & Keras Sequential Architecture¶

What this cell does: Defines the hyperparameter configuration for EXP-01-KERAS-BASELINE and builds the Keras model architecture from it (Pillar 1: Architecture).

How:

  • np.random.seed(42) / tf.random.set_seed(42) are re-applied here (not just once at the top of the notebook) so this specific run's weight initialization starts from the same fixed point regardless of what earlier experiment cells already ran and consumed random state from.
  • CONFIG bundles this run's hyperparameters: embed_dim=32 and hidden_dim=64 are Pillar 1 (Architecture); learning_rate=0.005, batch_size=32, epochs=15, optimizer_type="Adam" are Pillar 2 (Optimization); dropout_rate=0.1 is Pillar 3 (Regularization).
  • tf.keras.backend.clear_session() wipes any model/graph left behind by a previous cell, so re-running cells out of order can't leak weights between experiments.
  • Sequential() + Input(shape=(MAX_LEN,)) declares the model and forces Keras to build it immediately, so model.summary() later shows real shapes instead of ?.
  • Embedding(input_dim=len(vocab), output_dim=32, mask_zero=True) turns each integer token into a learned 32-length vector; mask_zero=True tells later layers to ignore <PAD> positions.
  • GlobalAveragePooling1D() averages those per-token vectors into one fixed-length vector per example — the automated feature-extraction step the lecture points to.
  • Dense(64, activation='relu') is the hidden layer doing the actual pattern learning.
  • Dropout(0.1) randomly zeroes hidden units during training to fight overfitting.
  • Dense(num_classes, activation='softmax') outputs a probability over the 3 sentiment classes.

Why: This is the required Task 1 baseline run, using the assignment's exact default settings (embed 32, hidden 64, LR 0.005, batch 32, epochs 15, dropout 0.1). Its job is to see whether an out-of-the-box Keras model already beats the PT-P1 no-code benchmark before any tuning happens.

Optimizer and Compilation & The Operational Loop (Fit & Evaluate)¶

What this cell does: Builds the optimizer, compiles the model, prints its summary, trains it, and computes the validation metrics logged for ?.

How:

  • The if/else on CONFIG["optimizer_type"] builds either an Adam or SGD optimizer object using this run's learning rate.
  • model.compile(loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', optimizer=opt, metrics=['accuracy']) — sparse categorical cross-entropy is used because the labels are plain integers (0/1/2), not one-hot vectors; accuracy is tracked per epoch alongside loss.
  • model.summary() prints the layer-by-layer shape/parameter table as a sanity check before training starts.
  • history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, validation_data=(X_val, y_val), epochs=..., batch_size=..., verbose=1) — this call is the training loop from the lecture: each epoch runs Forward Pass → Loss Calculation → Backward Pass → Weight Update over every mini-batch, then evaluates once on the validation set.
  • val_preds_probs = model.predict(X_val) → np.argmax(..., axis=1) converts the softmax probability vector for each example into a single predicted class (0, 1, or 2).
  • f1_score(y_val, val_preds, average='weighted') (plus precision_score/recall_score, same average='weighted') weights each class's contribution by how many examples it has — matching what the exercise deliverables table asks for ("Final Validation Weighted F1-Score").
  • val_loss = history.history['val_loss'][-1] takes the final epoch's validation loss, since this run doesn't use early stopping and always trains the full fixed epoch count.
  • The final print(...) writes one summary line the student copies into the Excel training log.

Why: This cell is where ? actually learns from data — the config/architecture cell above only sets the model up; this is what produces the val loss / F1 / precision / recall numbers that get compared against the PT-P1 benchmark and against every other run in the study.

Generate Loss Curves Chart¶

What this cell does: Plots training loss vs. validation loss per epoch for ? and saves the figure to Drive.

How:

  • train_losses/val_losses are pulled straight from history.history, the per-epoch log Keras kept during .fit() in the previous cell.
  • epochs_range = range(1, CONFIG['epochs'] + 1) — since this run doesn't use early stopping, the number of epochs plotted always matches the configured cap.
  • Two lines are plotted on the same axes: training loss (blue, solid, circle markers) and validation loss (red, dashed, square markers) — putting both on one chart is what makes over/underfitting visually obvious, per the lecture's "Diagnosing Model Fit" slide (converging together = good fit, diverging = overfitting, both flat and high = underfitting).
  • plt.savefig(f'{SAVE_DIR}/{CONFIG["run_id"]}_loss_curve.png', ...) writes a uniquely-named PNG for this run into the shared loss_curves Drive folder before plt.show() displays it inline, so every run's chart survives after the session ends.

Why: Task 3 explicitly requires saving a copy of each experiment's loss curve for the report, and this is the artifact used to classify ? as underfitting, overfitting, or a good fit when writing up Discussion Question 2.

Task 2: Systematic Experimentation & Outperforming PT-P1¶

Modify the HYPERPARAMETER CONFIGURATION to execute four (4) additional experiments (EXP-02 to EXP-05). The goal is to systematically iterate on the architecture and hyperparameters and observe if any model can exceed the PT-P1 baseline performance.

EXP-02-UNDERFITTING: Low Capacity & Too Small LR (Induce Underfitting)¶

What this cell does: Defines the hyperparameter configuration for EXP-02-UNDERFITTING and builds the Keras model architecture from it (Pillar 1: Architecture).

How:

  • np.random.seed(42) / tf.random.set_seed(42) are re-applied here (not just once at the top of the notebook) so this specific run's weight initialization starts from the same fixed point regardless of what earlier experiment cells already ran and consumed random state from.
  • CONFIG bundles this run's hyperparameters: embed_dim=32 and hidden_dim=16 are Pillar 1 (Architecture); learning_rate=0.0001, batch_size=32, epochs=15, optimizer_type="Adam" are Pillar 2 (Optimization); dropout_rate=0.0 is Pillar 3 (Regularization).
  • tf.keras.backend.clear_session() wipes any model/graph left behind by a previous cell, so re-running cells out of order can't leak weights between experiments.
  • Sequential() + Input(shape=(MAX_LEN,)) declares the model and forces Keras to build it immediately, so model.summary() later shows real shapes instead of ?.
  • Embedding(input_dim=len(vocab), output_dim=32, mask_zero=True) turns each integer token into a learned 32-length vector; mask_zero=True tells later layers to ignore <PAD> positions.
  • GlobalAveragePooling1D() averages those per-token vectors into one fixed-length vector per example — the automated feature-extraction step the lecture points to.
  • Dense(16, activation='relu') is the hidden layer doing the actual pattern learning.
  • Dropout(0.0) randomly zeroes hidden units during training to fight overfitting.
  • Dense(num_classes, activation='softmax') outputs a probability over the 3 sentiment classes.

Why: hidden_dim is dropped to 16 and learning_rate to 0.0001 on purpose — this is Task 2's “Low Capacity & Too Small LR (Induce Underfitting)” run. A hidden layer this small can't represent the sentiment patterns well, and a learning rate this small barely moves the weights each step, so the model should stay under-trained even after 15 epochs — the high-train-loss/high-val-loss signature the lecture describes for underfitting.

  • model.summary() prints the layer-by-layer shape/parameter table as a sanity check before training starts.
  • history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, validation_data=(X_val, y_val), epochs=..., batch_size=..., verbose=1) — this call is the training loop from the lecture: each epoch runs Forward Pass → Loss Calculation → Backward Pass → Weight Update over every mini-batch, then evaluates once on the validation set.
  • val_preds_probs = model.predict(X_val) → np.argmax(..., axis=1) converts the softmax probability vector for each example into a single predicted class (0, 1, or 2).
  • f1_score(y_val, val_preds, average='weighted') (plus precision_score/recall_score, same average='weighted') weights each class's contribution by how many examples it has — matching what the exercise deliverables table asks for ("Final Validation Weighted F1-Score").
  • val_loss = history.history['val_loss'][-1] takes the final epoch's validation loss, since this run doesn't use early stopping and always trains the full fixed epoch count.
  • The final print(...) writes one summary line the student copies into the Excel training log.

EXP-03-OVERFITTING: High Capacity & No Regularization (Induce Overfitting)¶

What this cell does: Defines the hyperparameter configuration for EXP-03-OVERFITTING and builds the Keras model architecture from it (Pillar 1: Architecture).

How:

  • np.random.seed(42) / tf.random.set_seed(42) are re-applied here (not just once at the top of the notebook) so this specific run's weight initialization starts from the same fixed point regardless of what earlier experiment cells already ran and consumed random state from.
  • CONFIG bundles this run's hyperparameters: embed_dim=32 and hidden_dim=256 are Pillar 1 (Architecture); learning_rate=0.05, batch_size=32, epochs=15, optimizer_type="Adam" are Pillar 2 (Optimization); dropout_rate=0.0 is Pillar 3 (Regularization).
  • tf.keras.backend.clear_session() wipes any model/graph left behind by a previous cell, so re-running cells out of order can't leak weights between experiments.
  • Sequential() + Input(shape=(MAX_LEN,)) declares the model and forces Keras to build it immediately, so model.summary() later shows real shapes instead of ?.
  • Embedding(input_dim=len(vocab), output_dim=32, mask_zero=True) turns each integer token into a learned 32-length vector; mask_zero=True tells later layers to ignore <PAD> positions.
  • GlobalAveragePooling1D() averages those per-token vectors into one fixed-length vector per example — the automated feature-extraction step the lecture points to.
  • Dense(256, activation='relu') is the hidden layer doing the actual pattern learning.
  • Dropout(0.0) randomly zeroes hidden units during training to fight overfitting.
  • Dense(num_classes, activation='softmax') outputs a probability over the 3 sentiment classes.

Why: hidden_dim is raised to 256, learning_rate to 0.05, and dropout_rate to 0 — deliberately maximizing capacity and optimization aggressiveness while removing the only regularization lever available, per Task 2's “High Capacity & No Regularization (Induce Overfitting)” spec. The model is expected to memorize the small training set almost immediately.

What this cell does: Builds the optimizer, compiles the model, prints its summary, trains it, and computes the validation metrics logged for EXP-03-OVERFITTING.

How:

  • The if/else on CONFIG["optimizer_type"] builds either an Adam or SGD optimizer object using this run's learning rate.
  • model.compile(loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', optimizer=opt, metrics=['accuracy']) — sparse categorical cross-entropy is used because the labels are plain integers (0/1/2), not one-hot vectors; accuracy is tracked per epoch alongside loss.
  • model.summary() prints the layer-by-layer shape/parameter table as a sanity check before training starts.
  • history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, validation_data=(X_val, y_val), epochs=..., batch_size=..., verbose=1) — this call is the training loop from the lecture: each epoch runs Forward Pass → Loss Calculation → Backward Pass → Weight Update over every mini-batch, then evaluates once on the validation set.
  • val_preds_probs = model.predict(X_val) → np.argmax(..., axis=1) converts the softmax probability vector for each example into a single predicted class (0, 1, or 2).
  • f1_score(y_val, val_preds, average='weighted') (plus precision_score/recall_score, same average='weighted') weights each class's contribution by how many examples it has — matching what the exercise deliverables table asks for ("Final Validation Weighted F1-Score").
  • val_loss = history.history['val_loss'][-1] takes the final epoch's validation loss, since this run doesn't use early stopping and always trains the full fixed epoch count.
  • The final print(...) writes one summary line the student copies into the Excel training log.

Why: This cell is where EXP-03-OVERFITTING actually learns from data — the config/architecture cell above only sets the model up; this is what produces the val loss / F1 / precision / recall numbers that get compared against the PT-P1 benchmark and against every other run in the study.

EXP-05-OPTIMAL: Optimal Model (Fine-tune to beat PT-P1)¶

What this cell does: Defines the hyperparameter configuration for EXP-05-OPTIMAL and builds the Keras model architecture from it (Pillar 1: Architecture).

How:

  • np.random.seed(42) / tf.random.set_seed(42) are re-applied here (not just once at the top of the notebook) so this specific run's weight initialization starts from the same fixed point regardless of what earlier experiment cells already ran and consumed random state from.
  • CONFIG bundles this run's hyperparameters: embed_dim=64 and hidden_dim=128 are Pillar 1 (Architecture); learning_rate=0.003, batch_size=32, epochs=15, optimizer_type="Adam" are Pillar 2 (Optimization); dropout_rate=0.3 is Pillar 3 (Regularization).
  • tf.keras.backend.clear_session() wipes any model/graph left behind by a previous cell, so re-running cells out of order can't leak weights between experiments.
  • Sequential() + Input(shape=(MAX_LEN,)) declares the model and forces Keras to build it immediately, so model.summary() later shows real shapes instead of ?.
  • Embedding(input_dim=len(vocab), output_dim=64, mask_zero=True) turns each integer token into a learned 64-length vector; mask_zero=True tells later layers to ignore <PAD> positions.
  • GlobalAveragePooling1D() averages those per-token vectors into one fixed-length vector per example — the automated feature-extraction step the lecture points to.
  • Dense(128, activation='relu') is the hidden layer doing the actual pattern learning.
  • Dropout(0.3) randomly zeroes hidden units during training to fight overfitting.
  • Dense(num_classes, activation='softmax') outputs a probability over the 3 sentiment classes.

Why: This fills Task 2's EXP-05 “Custom” slot — a hand-picked combination (embed 64, hidden 128, LR 0.003, dropout 0.3) sitting between EXP-01's plain baseline and EXP-04's heavier regularization, as a first tuned attempt before the systematic Task 4 ablations below.

What this cell does: Builds the optimizer, compiles the model, prints its summary, trains it, and computes the validation metrics logged for EXP-05-OPTIMAL.

How:

  • The if/else on CONFIG["optimizer_type"] builds either an Adam or SGD optimizer object using this run's learning rate.
  • model.compile(loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', optimizer=opt, metrics=['accuracy']) — sparse categorical cross-entropy is used because the labels are plain integers (0/1/2), not one-hot vectors; accuracy is tracked per epoch alongside loss.
  • model.summary() prints the layer-by-layer shape/parameter table as a sanity check before training starts.
  • history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, validation_data=(X_val, y_val), epochs=..., batch_size=..., verbose=1) — this call is the training loop from the lecture: each epoch runs Forward Pass → Loss Calculation → Backward Pass → Weight Update over every mini-batch, then evaluates once on the validation set.
  • val_preds_probs = model.predict(X_val) → np.argmax(..., axis=1) converts the softmax probability vector for each example into a single predicted class (0, 1, or 2).
  • f1_score(y_val, val_preds, average='weighted') (plus precision_score/recall_score, same average='weighted') weights each class's contribution by how many examples it has — matching what the exercise deliverables table asks for ("Final Validation Weighted F1-Score").
  • val_loss = history.history['val_loss'][-1] takes the final epoch's validation loss, since this run doesn't use early stopping and always trains the full fixed epoch count.
  • The final print(...) writes one summary line the student copies into the Excel training log.

Why: This cell is where EXP-05-OPTIMAL actually learns from data — the config/architecture cell above only sets the model up; this is what produces the val loss / F1 / precision / recall numbers that get compared against the PT-P1 benchmark and against every other run in the study.

Task 4: Free-Form Optimization & Maximum Performance Extraction¶

Each run below changes exactly one lever from the EXP-01 baseline configuration, so its effect can be judged in isolation before combining whichever changes actually helped into a final champion run. This keeps each result attributable to a specific cause rather than a bundle of simultaneous changes.

EXP-05A-EARLY-STOPPING: Baseline + Early Stopping¶

Isolates the effect of stopping training near the validation-loss minimum (observed around epoch 6-7 across EXP-01, EXP-04, and EXP-05) instead of training the full 15 epochs. All other hyperparameters match the EXP-01 baseline exactly, so any change in the result can be attributed to early stopping alone.

What this cell does: Defines the hyperparameter configuration for EXP-05A-EARLY-STOPPING and builds the Keras model architecture from it (Pillar 1: Architecture).

How:

  • np.random.seed(42) / tf.random.set_seed(42) are re-applied here (not just once at the top of the notebook) so this specific run's weight initialization starts from the same fixed point regardless of what earlier experiment cells already ran and consumed random state from.
  • CONFIG bundles this run's hyperparameters: embed_dim=32 and hidden_dim=64 are Pillar 1 (Architecture); learning_rate=0.005, batch_size=32, epochs=20, optimizer_type="Adam" are Pillar 2 (Optimization); dropout_rate=0.1 is Pillar 3 (Regularization).
  • patience: 3 is also set here, used by the EarlyStopping callback in the next cell.
  • tf.keras.backend.clear_session() wipes any model/graph left behind by a previous cell, so re-running cells out of order can't leak weights between experiments.
  • Sequential() + Input(shape=(MAX_LEN,)) declares the model and forces Keras to build it immediately, so model.summary() later shows real shapes instead of ?.
  • Embedding(input_dim=len(vocab), output_dim=32, mask_zero=True) turns each integer token into a learned 32-length vector; mask_zero=True tells later layers to ignore <PAD> positions.
  • GlobalAveragePooling1D() averages those per-token vectors into one fixed-length vector per example — the automated feature-extraction step the lecture points to.
  • Dense(64, activation='relu') is the hidden layer doing the actual pattern learning.
  • Dropout(0.1) randomly zeroes hidden units during training to fight overfitting.
  • Dense(num_classes, activation='softmax') outputs a probability over the 3 sentiment classes.

Why: Every hyperparameter matches the EXP-01 baseline exactly (embed 32, hidden 64, LR 0.005, dropout 0.1). The only changes are epochs raised to 20 (so EarlyStopping has room to trigger) and a patience key added. Holding everything else fixed means any F1/loss improvement over EXP-01 can be attributed specifically to early stopping, not to some other change.

What this cell does: Builds the optimizer, compiles the model, prints its summary, trains it, and computes the validation metrics logged for EXP-05A-EARLY-STOPPING.

How:

  • The if/else on CONFIG["optimizer_type"] builds either an Adam or SGD optimizer object using this run's learning rate.
  • model.compile(loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', optimizer=opt, metrics=['accuracy']) — sparse categorical cross-entropy is used because the labels are plain integers (0/1/2), not one-hot vectors; accuracy is tracked per epoch alongside loss.
  • model.summary() prints the layer-by-layer shape/parameter table as a sanity check before training starts.
  • EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss', patience=CONFIG['patience'], restore_best_weights=True) watches validation loss; if it doesn't improve for patience consecutive epochs, training stops and Keras rolls the model's weights back to whichever epoch had the lowest val_loss (not the last epoch run).
  • history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, validation_data=(X_val, y_val), epochs=..., batch_size=..., callbacks=[early_stop], verbose=1) — this call is the training loop from the lecture: each epoch runs Forward Pass → Loss Calculation → Backward Pass → Weight Update over every mini-batch, then evaluates once on the validation set.
  • val_preds_probs = model.predict(X_val) → np.argmax(..., axis=1) converts the softmax probability vector for each example into a single predicted class (0, 1, or 2).
  • f1_score(y_val, val_preds, average='weighted') (plus precision_score/recall_score, same average='weighted') weights each class's contribution by how many examples it has — matching what the exercise deliverables table asks for ("Final Validation Weighted F1-Score").
  • val_loss = min(history.history['val_loss']), not [-1] — because restore_best_weights=True means the model's actual weights come from the best epoch, so reporting the last epoch's logged loss would describe a model that's no longer in memory.
  • The final print(...) writes one summary line the student copies into the Excel training log.

Why: This cell is where EXP-05A-EARLY-STOPPING actually learns from data — the config/architecture cell above only sets the model up; this is what produces the val loss / F1 / precision / recall numbers that get compared against the PT-P1 benchmark and against every other run in the study.

EXP-05B-EXPANDED-DATA: Baseline + Dataset Expansion¶

Isolates the effect of adding more training data — combining the PT-P1 dataset with sample_dataset.csv (or additional written examples), keeping class balance — while holding every hyperparameter at the EXP-01 baseline values. Any change in the result can be attributed to the expanded dataset alone.

Fill in EXPANSION_CSV_FILEPATH below before running.

What this cell does: Builds the expanded training set for EXP-05B onward by combining the original PT-P1 dataset with the extra hand-written examples in pt_p1_dataset_expansion.csv, then rebuilds the vocabulary/encodings/splits on the combined data.

How:

  • EXPANSION_CSV_FILEPATH points at the second CSV of new examples.
  • pd.concat([df_original, df_expansion]) stacks the two DataFrames into one 452-row dataset.
  • The two print(...value_counts()) calls show the class balance before and after merging, so it's visible at a glance that the merge kept the classes roughly balanced (151/151/150) rather than skewing the model toward one label.
  • build_vocab / text_to_sequence / train_test_split are called again — identical logic to the very first data cell, just applied to df_combined — and the results overwrite the global vocab, X_data, y_data, X_train, X_val, X_test, num_classes that every cell below currently relies on, until they're reloaded again later.

Why: Task 4 explicitly lists "adding more training data instances" as one of the allowed free-form optimization levers, and PT-P1's own report found volume alone didn't fix its sarcasm/ ambiguity blind spot — it needed representative data covering the failure pattern. Keeping class balance while expanding avoids introducing a new bias in the process. The comment in the code flags on purpose that EXP-05C through EXP-05H all build on top of this expanded state, while EXP-05I/EXP-05J later reload data independently — that's intentional, so those two ablations aren't accidentally contaminated by whatever this cell left in memory.

  • The if/else on CONFIG["optimizer_type"] builds either an Adam or SGD optimizer object using this run's learning rate.
  • model.compile(loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', optimizer=opt, metrics=['accuracy']) — sparse categorical cross-entropy is used because the labels are plain integers (0/1/2), not one-hot vectors; accuracy is tracked per epoch alongside loss.
  • model.summary() prints the layer-by-layer shape/parameter table as a sanity check before training starts.
  • history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, validation_data=(X_val, y_val), epochs=..., batch_size=..., verbose=1) — this call is the training loop from the lecture: each epoch runs Forward Pass → Loss Calculation → Backward Pass → Weight Update over every mini-batch, then evaluates once on the validation set.
  • val_preds_probs = model.predict(X_val) → np.argmax(..., axis=1) converts the softmax probability vector for each example into a single predicted class (0, 1, or 2).
  • f1_score(y_val, val_preds, average='weighted') (plus precision_score/recall_score, same average='weighted') weights each class's contribution by how many examples it has — matching what the exercise deliverables table asks for ("Final Validation Weighted F1-Score").
  • val_loss = history.history['val_loss'][-1] takes the final epoch's validation loss, since this run doesn't use early stopping and always trains the full fixed epoch count.
  • The final print(...) writes one summary line the student copies into the Excel training log.

Why: This cell is where EXP-05B-EXPANDED-DATA actually learns from data — the config/architecture cell above only sets the model up; this is what produces the val loss / F1 / precision / recall numbers that get compared against the PT-P1 benchmark and against every other run in the study.

EXP-05C-COMBINED: Expanded Data + Early Stopping¶

Combines the two changes that each helped independently: EXP-05B's expanded dataset (better F1, still overfit) and EXP-05A's early stopping (contained overfitting, slightly lower F1). Tests whether stacking them produces a genuine champion result rather than either partial improvement alone.

Run this only after the EXP-05B data-expansion cell above has already executed in this session -- this cell trains on the same expanded X_train / X_val that EXP-05B built, it does not reload or re-expand the data itself.

What this cell does: Defines the hyperparameter configuration for EXP-05C-COMBINED and builds the Keras model architecture from it (Pillar 1: Architecture).

How:

  • np.random.seed(42) / tf.random.set_seed(42) are re-applied here (not just once at the top of the notebook) so this specific run's weight initialization starts from the same fixed point regardless of what earlier experiment cells already ran and consumed random state from.
  • CONFIG bundles this run's hyperparameters: embed_dim=32 and hidden_dim=64 are Pillar 1 (Architecture); learning_rate=0.005, batch_size=32, epochs=20, optimizer_type="Adam" are Pillar 2 (Optimization); dropout_rate=0.1 is Pillar 3 (Regularization).
  • patience: 3 is also set here, used by the EarlyStopping callback in the next cell.
  • tf.keras.backend.clear_session() wipes any model/graph left behind by a previous cell, so re-running cells out of order can't leak weights between experiments.
  • Sequential() + Input(shape=(MAX_LEN,)) declares the model and forces Keras to build it immediately, so model.summary() later shows real shapes instead of ?.
  • Embedding(input_dim=len(vocab), output_dim=32, mask_zero=True) turns each integer token into a learned 32-length vector; mask_zero=True tells later layers to ignore <PAD> positions.
  • GlobalAveragePooling1D() averages those per-token vectors into one fixed-length vector per example — the automated feature-extraction step the lecture points to.
  • Dense(64, activation='relu') is the hidden layer doing the actual pattern learning.
  • Dropout(0.1) randomly zeroes hidden units during training to fight overfitting.
  • Dense(num_classes, activation='softmax') outputs a probability over the 3 sentiment classes.

Why: Stacks the two changes that each helped independently — EXP-05A's early stopping and EXP-05B's expanded data — into one config (epochs raised to 20, patience added, trained on the expanded dataset). This becomes the shared baseline that EXP-05D through EXP-05J below each mutate by exactly one more variable.

What this cell does: Builds the optimizer, compiles the model, prints its summary, trains it, and computes the validation metrics logged for EXP-05C-COMBINED.

How:

  • The if/else on CONFIG["optimizer_type"] builds either an Adam or SGD optimizer object using this run's learning rate.
  • model.compile(loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', optimizer=opt, metrics=['accuracy']) — sparse categorical cross-entropy is used because the labels are plain integers (0/1/2), not one-hot vectors; accuracy is tracked per epoch alongside loss.
  • model.summary() prints the layer-by-layer shape/parameter table as a sanity check before training starts.
  • EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss', patience=CONFIG['patience'], restore_best_weights=True) watches validation loss; if it doesn't improve for patience consecutive epochs, training stops and Keras rolls the model's weights back to whichever epoch had the lowest val_loss (not the last epoch run).
  • history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, validation_data=(X_val, y_val), epochs=..., batch_size=..., callbacks=[early_stop], verbose=1) — this call is the training loop from the lecture: each epoch runs Forward Pass → Loss Calculation → Backward Pass → Weight Update over every mini-batch, then evaluates once on the validation set.
  • val_preds_probs = model.predict(X_val) → np.argmax(..., axis=1) converts the softmax probability vector for each example into a single predicted class (0, 1, or 2).
  • f1_score(y_val, val_preds, average='weighted') (plus precision_score/recall_score, same average='weighted') weights each class's contribution by how many examples it has — matching what the exercise deliverables table asks for ("Final Validation Weighted F1-Score").
  • val_loss = min(history.history['val_loss']), not [-1] — because restore_best_weights=True means the model's actual weights come from the best epoch, so reporting the last epoch's logged loss would describe a model that's no longer in memory.
  • The final print(...) writes one summary line the student copies into the Excel training log.

Why: This cell is where EXP-05C-COMBINED actually learns from data — the config/architecture cell above only sets the model up; this is what produces the val loss / F1 / precision / recall numbers that get compared against the PT-P1 benchmark and against every other run in the study.

EXP-05D-HIGHER-CAPACITY: EXP-05C + Increased Hidden Dimension¶

Starts from EXP-05C's setup (expanded data + early stopping) and changes exactly one more thing: hidden_dim 64 -> 128. Tests whether the ~14.6-point train/val accuracy gap remaining in EXP-05C is partly a capacity bottleneck -- i.e. whether the larger, more diverse dataset from EXP-05B can now support a bigger model without immediately overfitting past what early stopping can contain.

Run this only after the EXP-05B data-expansion cell has already executed in this session -- like EXP-05C, this trains on the same expanded X_train / X_val, it does not reload or re-expand the data itself.

EXP-05E-MORE-DROPOUT: EXP-05C + Increased Dropout¶

Starts from EXP-05C (expanded data + early stopping, hidden_dim=64) and changes exactly one more thing: dropout_rate 0.1 -> 0.3. EXP-05D already showed the remaining train/val gap isn't a capacity problem -- this tests whether it's a regularization problem instead. Directly answers Discussion Question 2 (how does dropout_rate affect over/underfitting).

Run this only after the EXP-05B data-expansion cell has already executed in this session.

What this cell does: Defines the hyperparameter configuration for EXP-05E-MORE-DROPOUT and builds the Keras model architecture from it (Pillar 1: Architecture).

How:

  • np.random.seed(42) / tf.random.set_seed(42) are re-applied here (not just once at the top of the notebook) so this specific run's weight initialization starts from the same fixed point regardless of what earlier experiment cells already ran and consumed random state from.
  • CONFIG bundles this run's hyperparameters: embed_dim=32 and hidden_dim=64 are Pillar 1 (Architecture); learning_rate=0.005, batch_size=32, epochs=20, optimizer_type="Adam" are Pillar 2 (Optimization); dropout_rate=0.3 is Pillar 3 (Regularization).
  • patience: 3 is also set here, used by the EarlyStopping callback in the next cell.
  • tf.keras.backend.clear_session() wipes any model/graph left behind by a previous cell, so re-running cells out of order can't leak weights between experiments.
  • Sequential() + Input(shape=(MAX_LEN,)) declares the model and forces Keras to build it immediately, so model.summary() later shows real shapes instead of ?.
  • Embedding(input_dim=len(vocab), output_dim=32, mask_zero=True) turns each integer token into a learned 32-length vector; mask_zero=True tells later layers to ignore <PAD> positions.
  • GlobalAveragePooling1D() averages those per-token vectors into one fixed-length vector per example — the automated feature-extraction step the lecture points to.
  • Dense(64, activation='relu') is the hidden layer doing the actual pattern learning.
  • Dropout(0.3) randomly zeroes hidden units during training to fight overfitting.
  • Dense(num_classes, activation='softmax') outputs a probability over the 3 sentiment classes.

Why: Identical to EXP-05C except dropout_rate: 0.1→0.3 — the only lever changed. Directly targets Discussion Question 2 (how dropout_rate affects over/underfitting) once early stopping and expanded data are already in place.

What this cell does: Builds the optimizer, compiles the model, prints its summary, trains it, and computes the validation metrics logged for EXP-05E-MORE-DROPOUT.

How:

  • The if/else on CONFIG["optimizer_type"] builds either an Adam or SGD optimizer object using this run's learning rate.
  • model.compile(loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', optimizer=opt, metrics=['accuracy']) — sparse categorical cross-entropy is used because the labels are plain integers (0/1/2), not one-hot vectors; accuracy is tracked per epoch alongside loss.
  • model.summary() prints the layer-by-layer shape/parameter table as a sanity check before training starts.
  • EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss', patience=CONFIG['patience'], restore_best_weights=True) watches validation loss; if it doesn't improve for patience consecutive epochs, training stops and Keras rolls the model's weights back to whichever epoch had the lowest val_loss (not the last epoch run).
  • history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, validation_data=(X_val, y_val), epochs=..., batch_size=..., callbacks=[early_stop], verbose=1) — this call is the training loop from the lecture: each epoch runs Forward Pass → Loss Calculation → Backward Pass → Weight Update over every mini-batch, then evaluates once on the validation set.
  • val_preds_probs = model.predict(X_val) → np.argmax(..., axis=1) converts the softmax probability vector for each example into a single predicted class (0, 1, or 2).
  • f1_score(y_val, val_preds, average='weighted') (plus precision_score/recall_score, same average='weighted') weights each class's contribution by how many examples it has — matching what the exercise deliverables table asks for ("Final Validation Weighted F1-Score").
  • val_loss = min(history.history['val_loss']), not [-1] — because restore_best_weights=True means the model's actual weights come from the best epoch, so reporting the last epoch's logged loss would describe a model that's no longer in memory.
  • The final print(...) writes one summary line the student copies into the Excel training log.

Why: This cell is where EXP-05E-MORE-DROPOUT actually learns from data — the config/architecture cell above only sets the model up; this is what produces the val loss / F1 / precision / recall numbers that get compared against the PT-P1 benchmark and against every other run in the study.

EXP-05F-LR-SCHEDULE: EXP-05C + Cosine Learning-Rate Decay¶

Starts from EXP-05C and replaces the flat learning rate with a cosine decay schedule -- every single run so far, including all of EXP-01 through EXP-05D, used a constant LR. The lecture (Pillar 2) specifically calls out schedules as improving training stability; this is the one lever from that section nothing has tested yet.

Run this only after the EXP-05B data-expansion cell has already executed in this session.

What this cell does: Defines the hyperparameter configuration for EXP-05F-LR-SCHEDULE and builds the Keras model architecture from it (Pillar 1: Architecture).

How:

  • np.random.seed(42) / tf.random.set_seed(42) are re-applied here (not just once at the top of the notebook) so this specific run's weight initialization starts from the same fixed point regardless of what earlier experiment cells already ran and consumed random state from.
  • CONFIG bundles this run's hyperparameters: embed_dim=32 and hidden_dim=64 are Pillar 1 (Architecture); initial_learning_rate=0.005, batch_size=32, epochs=20, optimizer_type="Adam" are Pillar 2 (Optimization); dropout_rate=0.1 is Pillar 3 (Regularization).
  • patience: 3 is also set here, used by the EarlyStopping callback in the next cell.
  • tf.keras.backend.clear_session() wipes any model/graph left behind by a previous cell, so re-running cells out of order can't leak weights between experiments.
  • Sequential() + Input(shape=(MAX_LEN,)) declares the model and forces Keras to build it immediately, so model.summary() later shows real shapes instead of ?.
  • Embedding(input_dim=len(vocab), output_dim=32, mask_zero=True) turns each integer token into a learned 32-length vector; mask_zero=True tells later layers to ignore <PAD> positions.
  • GlobalAveragePooling1D() averages those per-token vectors into one fixed-length vector per example — the automated feature-extraction step the lecture points to.
  • Dense(64, activation='relu') is the hidden layer doing the actual pattern learning.
  • Dropout(0.1) randomly zeroes hidden units during training to fight overfitting.
  • Dense(num_classes, activation='softmax') outputs a probability over the 3 sentiment classes.

Why: Same architecture as EXP-05C; the optimizer cell below replaces the flat learning rate with a cosine-decay schedule instead. Every prior run (EXP-01 through EXP-05D) used a constant LR the whole time — the lecture's Optimization pillar specifically calls out LR schedules as a stability lever nothing else here has tested yet.

What this cell does: Builds the optimizer, compiles the model, prints its summary, trains it, and computes the validation metrics logged for EXP-05F-LR-SCHEDULE.

How:

  • The if/else on CONFIG["optimizer_type"] builds either an Adam or SGD optimizer object using this run's learning rate.
  • The optimizer's learning rate is a CosineDecay schedule instead of a flat number: it starts at initial_learning_rate and smoothly decays toward 5% of that value (alpha=0.05) over the full training run, computed from steps_per_epoch × epochs.
  • model.compile(loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', optimizer=opt, metrics=['accuracy']) — sparse categorical cross-entropy is used because the labels are plain integers (0/1/2), not one-hot vectors; accuracy is tracked per epoch alongside loss.
  • model.summary() prints the layer-by-layer shape/parameter table as a sanity check before training starts.
  • EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss', patience=CONFIG['patience'], restore_best_weights=True) watches validation loss; if it doesn't improve for patience consecutive epochs, training stops and Keras rolls the model's weights back to whichever epoch had the lowest val_loss (not the last epoch run).
  • history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, validation_data=(X_val, y_val), epochs=..., batch_size=..., callbacks=[early_stop], verbose=1) — this call is the training loop from the lecture: each epoch runs Forward Pass → Loss Calculation → Backward Pass → Weight Update over every mini-batch, then evaluates once on the validation set.
  • val_preds_probs = model.predict(X_val) → np.argmax(..., axis=1) converts the softmax probability vector for each example into a single predicted class (0, 1, or 2).
  • f1_score(y_val, val_preds, average='weighted') (plus precision_score/recall_score, same average='weighted') weights each class's contribution by how many examples it has — matching what the exercise deliverables table asks for ("Final Validation Weighted F1-Score").
  • val_loss = min(history.history['val_loss']), not [-1] — because restore_best_weights=True means the model's actual weights come from the best epoch, so reporting the last epoch's logged loss would describe a model that's no longer in memory.
  • The final print(...) writes one summary line the student copies into the Excel training log.

Why: This cell is where EXP-05F-LR-SCHEDULE actually learns from data — the config/architecture cell above only sets the model up; this is what produces the val loss / F1 / precision / recall numbers that get compared against the PT-P1 benchmark and against every other run in the study.

EXP-05G-LARGER-VOCAB: EXP-05C + Increased MAX_VOCAB_SIZE¶

A quick check on the expanded (452-row) dataset found 1,377 unique word forms, but MAX_VOCAB_SIZE=1000 only keeps the top 998 (reserving 2 for <PAD>/<UNK>) -- meaning 379 unique words (about 27%) are currently collapsed into <UNK> every time they appear. This tests whether recovering that lost vocabulary signal improves the model.

Run this only after the EXP-05B data-expansion cell has already executed in this session -- this cell reuses df_combined (built there) rather than reloading data.

What this cell does: Rebuilds the vocabulary for EXP-05G with a higher size cap, to recover word coverage that was previously being lost.

How:

  • MAX_VOCAB_SIZE_V2 = 1500 replaces the original 1000-word cap.
  • vocab_before_size records the old vocab size purely so the printed comparison line is informative.
  • build_vocab / text_to_sequence / train_test_split are re-run on df_combined (the expanded dataset built by the EXP-05B data-expansion cell above), overwriting vocab/X_data/etc. again with the larger-vocabulary version.

Why: A quick audit of the expanded (452-row) dataset found 1,377 unique word forms, but the old MAX_VOCAB_SIZE=1000 only keeps the top 998 words (2 slots reserved for <PAD>/<UNK>) — meaning roughly 27% of unique words were being silently collapsed into <UNK> every time they appeared, discarding real signal. This cell tests whether recovering that lost vocabulary improves the model.

Vocabulary size: 1000 (MAX_VOCAB_SIZE=1000) -> 1379 (MAX_VOCAB_SIZE_V2=1500)
New split sizes -- Train: 316, Val: 68, Test: 68

What this cell does: Defines the hyperparameter configuration for EXP-05G-LARGER-VOCAB and builds the Keras model architecture from it (Pillar 1: Architecture).

How:

  • np.random.seed(42) / tf.random.set_seed(42) are re-applied here (not just once at the top of the notebook) so this specific run's weight initialization starts from the same fixed point regardless of what earlier experiment cells already ran and consumed random state from.
  • CONFIG bundles this run's hyperparameters: embed_dim=32 and hidden_dim=64 are Pillar 1 (Architecture); learning_rate=0.005, batch_size=32, epochs=20, optimizer_type="Adam" are Pillar 2 (Optimization); dropout_rate=0.1 is Pillar 3 (Regularization).
  • patience: 3 is also set here, used by the EarlyStopping callback in the next cell.
  • tf.keras.backend.clear_session() wipes any model/graph left behind by a previous cell, so re-running cells out of order can't leak weights between experiments.
  • Sequential() + Input(shape=(MAX_LEN,)) declares the model and forces Keras to build it immediately, so model.summary() later shows real shapes instead of ?.
  • Embedding(input_dim=len(vocab), output_dim=32, mask_zero=True) turns each integer token into a learned 32-length vector; mask_zero=True tells later layers to ignore <PAD> positions.
  • GlobalAveragePooling1D() averages those per-token vectors into one fixed-length vector per example — the automated feature-extraction step the lecture points to.
  • Dense(64, activation='relu') is the hidden layer doing the actual pattern learning.
  • Dropout(0.1) randomly zeroes hidden units during training to fight overfitting.
  • Dense(num_classes, activation='softmax') outputs a probability over the 3 sentiment classes.

Why: Same architecture and hyperparameters as EXP-05C; the only change (made in the cell above) is rebuilding the vocabulary with a higher cap so fewer real words get collapsed into <UNK>.

What this cell does: Builds the optimizer, compiles the model, prints its summary, trains it, and computes the validation metrics logged for EXP-05G-LARGER-VOCAB.

How:

  • The if/else on CONFIG["optimizer_type"] builds either an Adam or SGD optimizer object using this run's learning rate.
  • model.compile(loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', optimizer=opt, metrics=['accuracy']) — sparse categorical cross-entropy is used because the labels are plain integers (0/1/2), not one-hot vectors; accuracy is tracked per epoch alongside loss.
  • model.summary() prints the layer-by-layer shape/parameter table as a sanity check before training starts.
  • EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss', patience=CONFIG['patience'], restore_best_weights=True) watches validation loss; if it doesn't improve for patience consecutive epochs, training stops and Keras rolls the model's weights back to whichever epoch had the lowest val_loss (not the last epoch run).
  • history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, validation_data=(X_val, y_val), epochs=..., batch_size=..., callbacks=[early_stop], verbose=1) — this call is the training loop from the lecture: each epoch runs Forward Pass → Loss Calculation → Backward Pass → Weight Update over every mini-batch, then evaluates once on the validation set.
  • val_preds_probs = model.predict(X_val) → np.argmax(..., axis=1) converts the softmax probability vector for each example into a single predicted class (0, 1, or 2).
  • f1_score(y_val, val_preds, average='weighted') (plus precision_score/recall_score, same average='weighted') weights each class's contribution by how many examples it has — matching what the exercise deliverables table asks for ("Final Validation Weighted F1-Score").
  • val_loss = min(history.history['val_loss']), not [-1] — because restore_best_weights=True means the model's actual weights come from the best epoch, so reporting the last epoch's logged loss would describe a model that's no longer in memory.
  • The final print(...) writes one summary line the student copies into the Excel training log.

Why: This cell is where EXP-05G-LARGER-VOCAB actually learns from data — the config/architecture cell above only sets the model up; this is what produces the val loss / F1 / precision / recall numbers that get compared against the PT-P1 benchmark and against every other run in the study.

What this cell does: Plots training loss vs. validation loss per epoch for EXP-05G-LARGER-VOCAB and saves the figure to Drive.

How:

  • train_losses/val_losses are pulled straight from history.history, the per-epoch log Keras kept during .fit() in the previous cell.
  • epochs_range = range(1, len(train_losses) + 1) — uses the actual number of epochs completed (len(train_losses)), not CONFIG['epochs'], because EarlyStopping may have halted training before reaching the configured cap.
  • Two lines are plotted on the same axes: training loss (blue, solid, circle markers) and validation loss (red, dashed, square markers) — putting both on one chart is what makes over/underfitting visually obvious, per the lecture's "Diagnosing Model Fit" slide (converging together = good fit, diverging = overfitting, both flat and high = underfitting).
  • plt.savefig(f'{SAVE_DIR}/{CONFIG["run_id"]}_loss_curve.png', ...) writes a uniquely-named PNG for this run into the shared loss_curves Drive folder before plt.show() displays it inline, so every run's chart survives after the session ends.

Why: Task 3 explicitly requires saving a copy of each experiment's loss curve for the report, and this is the artifact used to classify EXP-05G-LARGER-VOCAB as underfitting, overfitting, or a good fit when writing up Discussion Question 2.

EXP-05H-SGD-OPTIMIZER: EXP-05C + SGD Optimizer (Isolate Optimizer Choice)¶

Every experiment so far uses Adam. This run keeps EXP-05C's config identical (expanded data, early stopping, same LR, same architecture) and changes only optimizer_type to "SGD", to see what Pillar 2's optimizer choice contributes on its own.

What this cell does: Defines the hyperparameter configuration for EXP-05H-SGD-OPTIMIZER and builds the Keras model architecture from it (Pillar 1: Architecture).

How:

  • np.random.seed(42) / tf.random.set_seed(42) are re-applied here (not just once at the top of the notebook) so this specific run's weight initialization starts from the same fixed point regardless of what earlier experiment cells already ran and consumed random state from.

EXP-05I-CAPACITY-ONLY: EXP-05D Architecture on Original (Non-Expanded) Data¶

Same architecture and hyperparameters as EXP-05D (hidden_dim 128, early stopping), but trained on the original dataset instead of the expanded one, to see how much of EXP-05D's performance came from capacity alone versus capacity + more data. Self-contained: this cell reloads and re-encodes the original CSV directly rather than relying on global state left behind by earlier cells, so it can be run on its own without executing EXP-05B/05C/etc. first (only the very first setup cell -- imports, Drive mount -- needs to have run).

What this cell does: For EXP-05I, reloads the original, non-expanded dataset directly from disk (rather than trusting whatever an earlier cell left in memory), then defines this run's hyperparameters and architecture.

How:

  • _df_original_only is a deliberately distinct, locally-scoped variable name (not df_original, which an earlier cell also defines) so this cell can't accidentally depend on state left behind by EXP-05B/EXP-05C/etc.
  • build_vocab / text_to_sequence / train_test_split are re-run on _df_original_only, producing a fresh vocab, X_train, X_val, etc. based only on the original 332-row dataset.
  • The CONFIG/architecture section below matches EXP-05D exactly (hidden_dim: 128, early stopping via patience) — the only thing different from EXP-05D is which dataset was used to build X_train/X_val above.

Why: This run exists specifically to isolate one variable: how much of EXP-05D's result came from the capacity increase (hidden_dim 64→128) alone, versus capacity combined with the expanded dataset. Making the cell self-contained (only requiring the very first setup cell to have run) is what makes that isolation trustworthy — it can't silently inherit the expanded dataset from an earlier cell in the session.

What this cell does: Plots training loss vs. validation loss per epoch for EXP-05I-CAPACITY-ONLY and saves the figure to Drive.

How:

  • train_losses/val_losses are pulled straight from history.history, the per-epoch log Keras kept during .fit() in the previous cell.
  • epochs_range = range(1, len(train_losses) + 1) — uses the actual number of epochs completed (len(train_losses)), not CONFIG['epochs'], because EarlyStopping may have halted training before reaching the configured cap.
  • Two lines are plotted on the same axes: training loss (blue, solid, circle markers) and validation loss (red, dashed, square markers) — putting both on one chart is what makes over/underfitting visually obvious, per the lecture's "Diagnosing Model Fit" slide (converging together = good fit, diverging = overfitting, both flat and high = underfitting).
  • plt.savefig(f'{SAVE_DIR}/{CONFIG["run_id"]}_loss_curve.png', ...) writes a uniquely-named PNG for this run into the shared loss_curves Drive folder before plt.show() displays it inline, so every run's chart survives after the session ends.

Why: Task 3 explicitly requires saving a copy of each experiment's loss curve for the report, and this is the artifact used to classify EXP-05I-CAPACITY-ONLY as underfitting, overfitting, or a good fit when writing up Discussion Question 2.

EXP-05J-BATCH-SIZE: EXP-05C + Smaller Batch Size (Isolate Batch Size)¶

Same config as EXP-05C (expanded data, early stopping, hidden_dim 64, LR 0.005, dropout 0.1) but with batch_size dropped from 32 to 16, to isolate the batch-size lever the lecture calls out under Pillar 2 (Optimization) -- the tradeoff between gradient noise, training speed, and generalization. Self-contained: rebuilds the expanded dataset directly from both CSVs rather than relying on state from earlier cells.

What this cell does: For EXP-05J, rebuilds the expanded (original + expansion) dataset directly from both CSVs on disk, independent of any state left behind by earlier cells, then defines this run's hyperparameters and architecture.

How:

  • _df_orig / _df_exp are read fresh from both CSV files and concatenated into _df_combined_local — all locally-scoped names, distinct from df_combined used elsewhere, so this cell can't accidentally depend on whether EXP-05B's data-expansion cell already ran in this session.
  • build_vocab / text_to_sequence / train_test_split rebuild vocab/X_train/X_val/etc. from that locally-built combined dataset.
  • The CONFIG/architecture section below matches EXP-05C exactly except batch_size: 32→16.

Why: Like EXP-05I, this keeps the batch-size ablation reproducible regardless of which earlier cells were or weren't executed — the whole point of this run is to isolate the effect of one smaller lever (batch size), so it can't be allowed to depend on fragile notebook execution order.

Expanded dataset -- Train: 316, Val: 68, Test: 68
Vocabulary size: 1000

What this cell does: Builds the optimizer, compiles the model, prints its summary, trains it, and computes the validation metrics logged for EXP-05J-BATCH-SIZE.

How:

  • The if/else on CONFIG["optimizer_type"] builds either an Adam or SGD optimizer object using this run's learning rate.
  • model.compile(loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', optimizer=opt, metrics=['accuracy']) — sparse categorical cross-entropy is used because the labels are plain integers (0/1/2), not one-hot vectors; accuracy is tracked per epoch alongside loss.
  • model.summary() prints the layer-by-layer shape/parameter table as a sanity check before training starts.
  • EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss', patience=CONFIG['patience'], restore_best_weights=True) watches validation loss; if it doesn't improve for patience consecutive epochs, training stops and Keras rolls the model's weights back to whichever epoch had the lowest val_loss (not the last epoch run).
  • history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, validation_data=(X_val, y_val), epochs=..., batch_size=..., callbacks=[early_stop], verbose=1) — this call is the training loop from the lecture: each epoch runs Forward Pass → Loss Calculation → Backward Pass → Weight Update over every mini-batch, then evaluates once on the validation set.
  • val_preds_probs = model.predict(X_val) → np.argmax(..., axis=1) converts the softmax probability vector for each example into a single predicted class (0, 1, or 2).
  • f1_score(y_val, val_preds, average='weighted') (plus precision_score/recall_score, same average='weighted') weights each class's contribution by how many examples it has — matching what the exercise deliverables table asks for ("Final Validation Weighted F1-Score").
  • val_loss = min(history.history['val_loss']), not [-1] — because restore_best_weights=True means the model's actual weights come from the best epoch, so reporting the last epoch's logged loss would describe a model that's no longer in memory.
  • The final print(...) writes one summary line the student copies into the Excel training log.

Why: This cell is where EXP-05J-BATCH-SIZE actually learns from data — the config/architecture cell above only sets the model up; this is what produces the val loss / F1 / precision / recall numbers that get compared against the PT-P1 benchmark and against every other run in the study.
